clinicalPearls: Presents with paroxysmal shooting or stabbing pain radiating from the suboccipital region up over the scalp in the distribution of the greater, lesser, or third occipital nerves
There is usually a background aching or dysaesthesia between paroxysms, with tenderness and a trigger point over the affected nerve at the occiput
Pressure over the greater occipital nerve where it emerges near the superior nuchal line often reproduces the pain
The affected scalp may show altered sensation (hyperaesthesia or hypoaesthesia), and allodynia to combing hair is common
A diagnostic and therapeutic occipital nerve block that abolishes the pain confirms the diagnosis
It must be distinguished from referred pain from the upper cervical spine and from primary headaches such as migraine and cervicogenic headache
Treatment ranges from local measures, neuropathic agents (including carbamazepine and amitriptyline), and occipital nerve blocks to neurostimulation or surgical decompression in refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Occipital neuralgia is caused by irritation, entrapment, or injury of the greater, lesser, or third occipital nerves, which arise from the upper cervical (chiefly C2) roots. Compression as the nerve passes through the suboccipital muscles and fascia, degenerative change or instability of the upper cervical spine, or local trauma provoke ectopic discharges and pain referred throughout the nerve's cutaneous territory over the posterior scalp. Convergence of upper cervical and trigeminal afferents in the trigeminocervical complex explains why pain may also be felt in frontal and periorbital regions.
additionalDifferentials: Upper cervical spine degenerative or facet disease
Posterior fossa or craniocervical junction lesion
additionalInvestigations: Palpation for an occipital trigger point reproducing the pain
Diagnostic occipital nerve block with local anaesthetic
MRI or CT of the cervical spine and craniocervical junction when a structural cause is suspected
Inflammatory markers to exclude giant cell arteritis in older patients
Neurological examination of the upper limbs and cranial nerves
Imaging of the posterior fossa if central pathology is suspected
redFlags: New occipital pain in an older patient with jaw claudication or visual symptoms suggesting giant cell arteritis
Associated neurological deficit or myelopathic signs pointing to a craniocervical lesion
Systemic features such as fever or weight loss
Progressive, unremitting pain unresponsive to nerve block
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and frequently responds to conservative measures and occipital nerve blocks, though relapses are common. Refractory cases can be helped by neurostimulation or surgical decompression, and any underlying cervical pathology should be addressed.
pitfalls: Confusing occipital neuralgia with migraine or cervicogenic headache
Missing giant cell arteritis in an older patient with occipital scalp pain
Overlooking upper cervical spine pathology as the underlying cause
Failing to confirm the diagnosis with a nerve block before invasive treatment
Attributing frontal or periorbital pain to another disorder when it reflects trigeminocervical convergence
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: First-line conservative care with rest, local heat, massage, physiotherapy and correction of cervical posture
Neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy using anticonvulsants such as gabapentinoids or carbamazepine, or a tricyclic antidepressant, with simple analgesics or muscle relaxants for the background ache
Diagnostic and therapeutic greater, lesser or third occipital nerve block with local anaesthetic and corticosteroid
Identification and treatment of any underlying upper cervical spine pathology or instability
For refractory pain, escalation to pulsed radiofrequency, occipital nerve stimulation or surgical decompression and neurolysis
Exclusion and treatment of giant cell arteritis in older patients with new occipital pain before attributing symptoms to neuralgia
